newsitem.title: GERMANY: Financial leaders head to Berlin as dollar surges.
newsitem.headline: Financial leaders head to Berlin as dollar surges.

text.p: Foreign exchange markets pitted their collective will against the world's financial leaders on Friday, pushing the U.S. dollar to 32-month highs even as the top monetary officials headed to Berlin for a summit meeting.

Currency issues look set to dominate Saturday's talks among Group of Seven finance ministers and central bank governors, with a rapid surge in the dollar last month vying for attention with a simmering row over Europe's single currency plans.

Other agenda items -- world growth, debt relief to the world's poorest countries and cooperation between supervisory authorities -- are expected to gain scant attention, with nations already sharing broad agreement on these topics.

On the dollar, the dilemma facing the leaders will be how to at once welcome the currency' recovery from 1995 lows, which the G7 itself has fostered, without sending a signal to the market which could prompt a further surge or a slide lower.

"Their aim will be to try to smooth the market movements," Eckhard Schulte, economist at the Industrial Bank of Japan in Frankfurt, said of the Group of Seven that comprises Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.
"They want to see a more gradual movement," he added.

In a measure of the current sensitivity of markets to any G7 official's view on currencies, Friday's surge was triggered by German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who said the strong dollar helped boost German exports, posed no inflation risk and that there was no need for the G7 to set exchange rate targets.
Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher gave the dollar a further nudge up when he told reporters the German central bank was satisfied with current dollar exchange rates.

While the U.S. and France in particular have joined Germany in welcoming the dollar's rise, Japan, which has seen the yen fall by over 50 percent against the dollar in the last 22 months, has expressed repeated concern about the rapid move in currency rates and called for G7 action against it.
Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka repeated on Friday that he would be stressing the need for exchange rate stability at the meeting.

Even International Monetary Fund head Michel Camdessus, who this week said currency levels were extremely favourable, warned on Friday that the yen should not be allowed to fall so far as to force Japan to raise interest rates.
But the dollar issue is just one of two key currency questions facing the G7 meeting.

With Europe's single currency, the euro, placed high on the agenda by the host minister, Waigel, the talks will inevitably touch on a dispute this week over whether some European nations were seeking a deal to delay the entry of others to monetary union.
Europe plans to launch its single currency from 1999, melding the currencies of all nations which want to do so and which can prove they have achieved economic stability by meeting set goals.

But a report this week -- heavily denied by officials -- said a deal had been made to offer only a late entry pass to Italy and other nations which have staged a belated sprint to reach these economic targets, raising worries about their ability to sustain healthy economies.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi, holding a summit meeting in Bonn, were expected to try to smooth ruffled diplomatic feathers in advance of the G7 talks.
Italian foreign minister Lamberto Dini, in Bonn for the German-Italian consultations, told reporters on the sidelines of the talks, "Germany believes in a strong and large European currency union."
